name: Bianca Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi, Bianca, thanks for doing this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you take me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a line operator at Varden Electronics, in the business park off the motorway. We make circuit boards for heat pumps. I run the pick-and-place machines, which put tiny parts onto the boards at crazy speed, and the reflow oven that melts the solder. My day is loading reels of parts, checking the first board of every batch under the microscope, and sorting out the machine when it drops a part. Five years there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's precise, and I like the machines. I use an AI assistant every day, to read error logs, to write setup checklists, even to help me learn a bit of Python in the evenings. What wears me out is the twelve-hour shifts on the four-on, four-off rota. My boyfriend Kofi is a software tester at an insurance company, so he's home by six every day and I'm the one with the weird hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, which is more or less what I think now. At work I'd show people the shortcuts that do help. Online I'd probably not bother saying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's pretty much fine. My job is very hands-on, and the machines are already automated, they just need someone like me to keep them fed and fix them. I'd carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using AI for logs and checklists, and maybe finally apply for the process technician job at Varden, which pays about fifteen percent more. Keep putting money in my savings and the index fund. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost a bit disappointed, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. Would anything change for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The AI tools would stay handy, like a good calculator. I'd keep using them for the boring bits, like logging downtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi would be fine too. His testing work would just get a bit faster with the tools. I think he'd be relieved.

At work I'd show people the **shortcuts** that genuinely help.
think: My job is **hands-on**, feeding and fixing already automated machines.
The **process technician** promotion would still be my next step.
do: Keep using AI for **error logs** and setup checklists.
Apply for the **process technician** job, about fifteen percent more pay.
Keep paying into savings and the **index fund**.
S0.quote: The AI tools would stay handy, like a good calculator.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **daily** and sees it as a practical tool.
A **promotion** to process technician is her next step regardless.
In this world her partner's **desk job** feels safe too.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for error logs and checklists
Apply for the process technician job at Varden
Keep paying into the index fund monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a normal shift, like when factories got computers. People who learn to use it will be fine. I'd say it at work, but nicely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm OK, but Kofi's job is right in the line of fire. Testing software and checking things is the first thing on the card. I'd worry for our household more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the process technician job straight away. I'd ask Varden to send me on an automation course, and I'd use AI even more at work. I'd sit down with Kofi and help him find what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for Kofi and for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Kofi tests software. How does this picture land for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He already says the tools write half the tests now. In a year or two, the company might keep one tester where they had four. I think he'd be one of the ones they keep, but I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for AI or robots at Varden yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We still check circuit boards by eye under the microscope, and a vision system with AI would catch more defects. I'd write the proposal myself and ask to run the trial.

Propose an **AI vision system** to check boards.
feel: **Uneasy**, for Kofi and for the two of them.

She'd actively **bring in automation** at her own plant.
She sees steady change as a **promotion chance** for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be practical. Governments should get ready with support for people who lose jobs. I'd say that at work and to friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Kofi's job goes in 2028, and mine goes around 2031 when robots can do my hands-on work. The pick-and-place machines are already half robots. I'd have three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to a company that installs and sets up automation lines, because they'll be busy until 2031. I'd save every spare penny. And I'd help Kofi find a hands-on trade, maybe as an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Kofi actually say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd do a spreadsheet at the kitchen table: two jobs, one gone in 2028, one gone in 2031. We'd be fine for a while with savings, but we'd have to decide which of us retrains first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does that help you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me move fast, but in this picture AI does my thinking work by 2028 anyway. What helps is my hands and the three years. I'd use those years to earn and save as much as I can.

say: Governments should prepare **support** for people who lose jobs.
I'd tell friends to **plan now** rather than hope it passes.
think: Kofi's job goes in **2028** and mine around **2031**.
The **pick-and-place machines** are already half robots.
That leaves me about **three years** to earn and save.
do: Move to an **automation installer** that'll be busy until 2031.
Help Kofi find a **hands-on trade**, maybe electrician.
S2.quote: We'd do a spreadsheet at the kitchen table: two jobs, one gone in 2028, one gone in 2031.
fieldNote: She meets the shock with **planning**, literally a spreadsheet.
Her **daily AI use** helps her move fast but doesn't protect her job.
The **three-year gap** between AI and robots is her earning window.

steps.text: Move to a firm that installs automation lines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but not to waste. Companies and schools should start training people now. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have about eight years, until 2034. That's enough to move up and into setting up the robots, not just running machines. Kofi would have five years to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time two-year diploma in automation, starting next autumn. Kofi would start his trade course straight away. I'd keep investing, because there's time for it to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you put your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the index fund, plus a bit into the companies that make the robots. If robots take my job, I might as well own a little piece of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Kofi take the idea of a trade course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi would complain, then do it. He's good with his hands, he fixes everyone's bikes.

I'd say it at work and **online**, plainly.
think: That's enough to move into **setting up robots**, not just running machines.
do: Start a part-time **automation diploma** next autumn.
Support Kofi starting a **trade course** straight away.
S3.quote: If robots take my job, I might as well own a little piece of the robots.
fieldNote: She'd **invest in robot makers** as a hedge against her own job.
She plans both her own and her partner's **retraining**.
Five years turns her from **anxious** to uneasy.

steps.text: Start a part-time automation diploma next autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly. No need to panic. Everyone should start learning slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. I'd be a robot technician or similar long before 2039, and by then I'd have a good pile saved. I'd still be young enough to switch again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using AI, finish the diploma over the next three years, and move into automation. Keep investing. Maybe help Kofi think about his next step, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relaxed, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people get lazy because ten years sounds like forever. I've seen that at Varden with every change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. I'd just start the diploma a year earlier than I was going to.

say: Ten years is enough to **plan properly**.
Everyone should start **learning slowly**, without panic.
I'd say that calmly at **work**, not as a warning.
think: I'd be a **robot technician** long before 2039.
I'd have a **good pile saved** and be young enough to switch again.
do: Finish an **automation diploma** over the next three years.
Start the diploma a **year earlier** than planned.
S4.quote: People get lazy because ten years sounds like forever.
fieldNote: A decade feels like **plenty** for someone this adaptable and well saved.
Her only worry is colleagues' **complacency**, which she has seen at Varden before.
She'd start retraining **earlier** rather than later.

steps.text: Start the automation diploma a year earlier than planned
Keep investing in the index fund every month
Keep using AI for logs and setup at Varden

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Kofi and I lose our jobs three years apart and there's no time to do it properly. What would help is fast, cheap automation courses, and some kind of income support while people switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about who gets the new jobs. The jobs setting up robots will go to people who already know the machines. Operators like me should be first in line for the robot jobs, not people hired from outside.

headlineQuote: Operators like me should be first in line for the robot jobs, not people hired from outside.
portrait: Bianca, 27, runs **pick-and-place machines** making circuit boards and uses AI every day.
She's practical and moves fast, aiming to become a **process or automation** technician.
Her boyfriend Kofi tests software, so his **desk job** is the household's first risk.
She's calm in slow worlds and **anxious** in AGI by 2028, but always plans.
She'd **invest in robot makers** and push to automate inspection at her own plant.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Kofi lose jobs three years apart with no time.
